pitchei_teshuva.en:
He receives forty lashes. See Tosafot, Kiddushin 28a, who explain that this is measure for measure: he said that his fellow had violated a prohibition, and therefore he himself is punished accordingly; see there. Magen Avraham, siman 610, seif katan 6, explains that the relevant prohibition is “A mamzer shall not enter” the congregation; see there and Machatzit HaShekel. Responsa Chatam Sofer, Choshen Mishpat, siman 181, writes that one should not ask what this means when the person shamed is unmarried, because the slanderer at least seeks to bring him to lashes once he marries. This is also explicit in Yam Shel Shlomo, Bava Kamma, chapter 8, siman 44; see there. Yam Shel Shlomo further writes that the rule of lashes is not limited to one who calls another a mamzer. Rather, it applies to any defamatory accusation that alleges violation of a prohibition. Chatam Sofer comments that, but for those words, he would have said that if one tells another, “You ate forbidden fat,” or the like, perhaps the person has already repented; likewise, the ancestors of a mamzer may have acted under compulsion or repented. The status of mamzer, however, is an enduring blemish, and the slanderer thereby suspects him of being destined continually to violate the prohibition against entering the congregation whenever he marries. Chatam Sofer further writes that the lashes are customarily redeemed with money. Mahari Weil states that the amount is forty gold coins, and the Rama likewise rules at the end of siman 2. Yam Shel Shlomo, Bava Kamma, chapter 8, siman 49, writes that he found in the name of earlier authorities that the lashes are redeemed for eight Rhenish gold coins, and that this custom has the force of law even against the wishes of the person who was shamed. The printed text there reading five Rhenish gold coins is in fact a scribal error and should read eight Rhenish gold coins, as is also evident from Responsa Maharshal, siman 101, where he counts eight gold coins. See also Responsa Nachalat Shivah, part II, end of siman 66. Yam Shel Shlomo further protests the custom of distributing the fine to yeshivah students or the like. He rules that anyone who sees his work should tell the person who was shamed that the money belongs to him and that he may do with it as he wishes. Mahari Weil, however, at the end of siman 147, rules that the offender should give forty gold coins to charity, while the person who was shamed chooses how they are to be distributed. It appears to me that there is no dispute. When the offender impugned the honor of the person himself, the money belongs to that person, and he may even spend it on drink, as Maharshal writes. But where the offender impugned the honor of his ancestors, the descendant should not eat and rejoice from the degradation of his forebears. Rather, so that the payment should serve as atonement for the offender, the money should be distributed to charity for the benefit of the souls of those who repose in the earth. Nevertheless, the right to designate the recipients belongs to the son, who stands as their blood-avenger. Mahari Weil is explicitly discussing such a case. See further there. See also Atzmot Yosef on Kiddushin there, who cites a responsum of Ri Migash: if one called another “mamzer, son of a mamzer,” he incurs two sets of lashes; but if he said, “Your father and you are mamzerim,” he incurs only one set. The reason is that it is known that if a man is a mamzer, his son and descendants remain mamzerim through all generations. Thus, once he first calls the father a mamzer, he has already necessarily characterized the son and descendants as mamzerim. But if he first calls the son a mamzer, it remains possible that the father is fit; when he then adds the separate insult that the father too is a mamzer, he incurs a second liability. See there.
He receives forty lashes. See Tosafos to Kiddushin 28a, who writes that this is measure for measure: he says that his fellow violated a negative commandment, and therefore, etc.; see there. In Magen Avraham, siman 610, seif katan 6, it is explained that this refers to the prohibition, "A mamzer shall not enter," etc.; see there and Machatzis HaShekel ad loc. See Responsa Chatam Sofer, Choshen Mishpat, siman 181, who writes that one should not object that, if so, what can be said where one humiliates an unmarried man. One can answer that, in any event, he seeks to bring him to liability for lashes when he marries a woman. This is also explicit in Yam Shel Shlomo, Bava Kamma, chapter 8, siman 44; see there. Yam Shel Shlomo there further writes that the rule of lashes does not apply only to one who calls another a mamzer, but to every defamatory accusation that entails a negative prohibition. Chatam Sofer there comments that, were it not for his words, he would have said that where one tells another, "You ate forbidden fat," and the like, perhaps he already repented; likewise, the ancestors of a mamzer may have acted under duress or repented. By contrast, the status of mamzer is a continuing blemish, and he thereby suspects him of being destined to violate the prohibition of "shall not enter" whenever he marries a woman. Chatam Sofer there further writes that the lashes are customarily redeemed with money. Mahariv writes that the amount is forty gold coins, and so writes Rama in Shulchan Aruch at the end of siman 2, etc. In Yam Shel Shlomo, Bava Kamma, chapter 8, siman 49, he writes that he found in the name of the great authorities that the lashes are redeemed with five Rhenish gold coins, and that this custom has the force of law even against the will of the person who was humiliated. In truth, this is a scribal error in Yam Shel Shlomo, and it should read eight Rhenish gold coins; so too in Responsa Maharshal, siman 101, it states eight gold coins, etc. See also Responsa Nachalas Shivah, part 2, end of siman 66. I further saw in Yam Shel Shlomo there that he protests the practice of distributing the fine to yeshiva students and the like, and he charges anyone who sees his work to tell the person who was humiliated that the money is his and that he may do with it whatever he wishes. Mahariv, however, at the end of siman 147, rules that he should give forty gold coins to charity, with the person who was humiliated choosing what is to be done with them. It appears to me that there is no dispute. Certainly, where the insult was to the honor of the humiliated person himself, the money belongs to him, and he may even use it to drink beer, as Maharshal rules. But where the insult was to the honor of his ancestors, he should not eat and rejoice from the humiliation of his ancestors. Rather, so that there be atonement for the offender, the money should be distributed to charity for the souls of those who dwell in the dust. Nevertheless, the benefit of directing the distribution belongs to the son, for he is their avenger of blood. Mahariv there is explicitly discussing such a case. These are his words; see there further. See also Atzmos Yosef to Kiddushin there, who cites the responsum of Ri Migash, of blessed memory, that if one called another "a mamzer, son of a mamzer," he is liable twice; but if he said to him, "Your father and you are mamzerim," he is liable only for one set of lashes. The reason is that it is known that when a man is a mamzer, his son and his descendants to the end of all generations are mamzerim. Therefore, once he first called the father a mamzer, he thereby necessarily characterized his offspring as mamzerim. But if he first called the son a mamzer, it is possible that the father is legitimate; when he then added the insult to the father by saying that he is the son of a mamzer, he incurs two sets of lashes. See there.

mechaber.he: כל אלו הסלעים הם מכסף מדינה שאין בו כסף אלא שמינית שהם שלש מעין שכל מעה משקל ט"ז שעורות כסף צרוף שהוא עוטמני א':
mechaber.en: These are all the rocks from state money that does not have money, but rather that it is a sort of thing that every weight of a drone that hides money that is eccentric:

beer_hagolah.he: ס) איבעי' בגמרא שם ד' צ' ע"ב ונפשטא מימרא דרב יהודה א"ר כל כסף האמור בתורה כסף צורי ושל דבריהם כסף מדינה בפ"ד דף ל"ו ע"ב וכ"כ הרמב"ם שם בפ"ג ד"י כל אנו הסלעים הם מכסף א"י באותו הזמן שהיה בכל סלע חצי דינר כסף וג' דינרים ומחצה נחושת וכו'
beer_hagolah.en: This was an unresolved question in the Gemara there, 90b, and was resolved from Rav Yehudah in the name of Rav: every mention of money in the Torah means Tyrian currency, while rabbinic amounts mean provincial currency, Bava Kamma chapter 4, 36b. Rambam likewise writes in chapter 3, law 10, that these sela'im are of the silver currency of Eretz Yisrael at that time, each sela containing half a dinar of silver and three and a half dinars of copper, etc.

beur_hagra.he:
כל אלו כו'. ל"ו ב':
(ליקוט) שאין בו כסף כו'. כמ"ש ברפ"ד שסלע הוא פלגא דזוזא (ע"כ):
(ליקוט) שכל מעה כו'. כמ"ש הרי"ף ורא"ש בריש קדושין ע"ש ועי"ד ר"ס רצ"ד וסי' ש"ד (ע"כ):
beur_hagra.en:
All of this is so. B:
He has no money. It is like a rock that is a rock
(Supplement) Every ma'ah, etc. This is as Rif and Rosh write at the beginning of Kiddushin. See Yoreh Deah 294 and 304.

meirat_einayim.he: אלא שמינית כו' ז"ל הטור והרמב"ם סלע מדינה יש בו חצי דינר כסף (שהוא שמינית שבסלע צורי שיש בו ד' דינרי כסף) וג' דינרים ומחצה נחושת לפיכך מי שנתחייב ק' סלעי' משלם י"ב סלעי' ומחצה כסף נקי עכ"ל ובפרישה כתבתי דאינו ר"ל דיצא בשילום י"ב סלעי' והחצי כסף נקי לחוד שהרי כיון דחייבוהו לשלם בסלעים שבכל סלע יש בו ז' חלקים נחשת והחלק השמיני של כסף נהי דנסתלק ממנו בזה ידי שלום הכסף שבו עדיין לא נסתלק ממנו תשלומין הנחשת שבו וצ"ל דמ"ש דמשלם י"ב סלעי' ומחצה כו' צ"ל כשיבא לשלם לו בסלעי' דמדינה ירא' שלא יהא בהן פחות מי"ב סלעים ומחצה כסף והמותר יהיה נחשת ומשום דהמקומות והזמנים משתנים שפוחתין בסלע מדינה הכסף ומוסיפין במקומו נחשת מ"ה כתב שיעור הכסף שלא יפחות מזה ומה"נ נראה דסתם המחבר ולא כתב שיתן י"ב סלעים ומחצה כסף כי לא בא אלא ללמדינו כמה כסף יהיה בו והרמב"ם שכתבו בספ"ג דחובל מ"מ רמזו במה שהתחיל שם וכתב ז"ל כל אלו הסלעים הן מכסף א"י באותו זמן שהיה בכל סלע כו' חצי דינר כסף כו' הרי לשונו משמע שבא ללמדינו כמה היה הסלע באותו זמן דחכמי המשנ' שקבעו שיעורים הללו ומאותו שיעור נלמד לכל זמן וזמן ומקום ומקום לפי מה שהוא המטבע שם שלא יפחות הכסף ממנו וכנ"ל ועמ"ש בפריש' עוד מזה:
meirat_einayim.en: Only one eighth, etc. The Tur and Rambam write that a provincial sela contains half a dinar of silver, which is one eighth of a Tyrian sela containing four silver dinars, and three and a half dinars of copper. Therefore, one who is obligated to pay one hundred sela'im pays twelve and a half sela'im of pure silver. In Perishah I explained that this does not mean he fulfills his entire obligation merely by paying twelve and a half pure silver sela'im. Since he was obligated in provincial sela'im, each containing seven parts copper and one part silver, payment of the silver component does not discharge the copper component. Rather, the statement means that when he pays in provincial sela'im, he must ensure that they contain no less than the equivalent of twelve and a half sela'im of silver, with the remainder made up of copper. Because places and periods differ, and the silver content of the provincial sela may be reduced while copper is added, the authorities stated the minimum silver content so that it not fall below this amount. This also explains why the Mechaber simply states the ratio and does not instruct him to give twelve and a half silver sela'im. His purpose is only to teach how much silver the coin must contain. Rambam, at the end of chapter 3 of Hilchot Chovel, likewise hints to this by beginning: "All these sela'im are of the coinage of Eretz Yisrael at that time, when each sela contained... half a dinar of silver," etc. His wording shows that he is teaching the composition of the coin in the era when the Sages of the Mishnah fixed these amounts. From that standard we learn for every later time and place according to the local coinage, provided its silver content is not less than this amount. See Perishah for further discussion.

mechaber.he: בד"א במכובד אבל אדם שהוא מבוזה ואינו מקפיד בכל אלו הדברים וכיוצא בהם אינו אלא כפי מה שיראו הדיינים שראוי ליטול: הגה י"א שאלו הדברים אינן רק משום בושת וצער אבל ריפוי ושבת הכל לפי הענין (טור סל"ד בשם הרי"ף וכ"כ הרא"ש בשמו):
mechaber.en: The foregoing fixed assessments apply to a person of standing. With a degraded person who is not particular about such humiliations and similar matters, the amount is only what the judges consider appropriate for him to receive. <small>Rama: Some say these assessments concern only humiliation and pain, while medical expenses and loss of work are always assessed according to the actual circumstances. Tur, seif 34, in the name of Rif; Rosh likewise writes this in Rif's name.</small>

beer_hagolah.he:
ע) שם די"א כ' ה"ה חלוק זה מכל האמורין מתקע חבירו עד כאן מפיר' במשנה שם כתנא קמא דר"ע (מפרש בגמ' דף צ"א ע"א) אבל אג' הראשונים אינם מפורשי' אם הם במכובד דוקא ודעת רבינו להשוותן ונכון הוא (וכ"כ התוספת בשם ר"י שם סוף דף כ"ז)
פ) וכ"כ ה"ה שם ד"ח בשם קצת המפרשים וכן פירש"י ז"ל שם
beer_hagolah.en:
There, law 11. The Maggid Mishneh writes that this distinction, from one who strikes his fellow through this point, is explicit in the Mishnah following the first Tanna against Rabbi Akiva, as explained in the Gemara 91a. But the first three categories are not explicit as applying only to a person of stature. Rambam equates them, which is correct. Tosafot likewise write so in the name of Ri at the end of 27b.
The Maggid Mishneh likewise writes there, law 8, in the name of some commentators. Rashi also explains so there.

beer_hagolah.en: Beit Yosef writes that in the Rif text in our possession it states that he agreed with the other Rabbis that this entire sum is the victim's. Thus he explicitly agrees with Rambam, and we rule accordingly, especially because the law is to retain money in possession. Beit Yosef further writes that if the person struck him with such force that the blow caused substantial physical damage, it appears Rambam would agree that medical expenses and loss of labor are also paid.
